These three presented the program, Miss Baum playing "Nocturne in E Minor" (Chopin) and "In Autumn" (Moszkowski), Miss Smith, "Sonata in F Flat Minor" (Chopin), and Miss Michaelson, two Chopin selections, "Nocturne in G Sharp Minor" and "Scherzo in B Minor."

Miss Michaelson also gave an interesting talk on the course in managerial work for Settlement Music Schools, from which she is to be graduated in June. She has the honor of being the first musician to be financed by the Juilliard Foundation for this course.

Other "home-coming" members at this time were Beatrice Wilson Baker and Ann Keliher from New York and Helen Williams and Edward Dawson from Baltimore. The event was held at the home of the club's founder and director, Mrs. Martin A. Morrison. About 40 members attended.

CARTHAGE, Tunisia, May — Catholics from all over the world are converging this week on Carthage—now a little town of 200 houses, but once the greatest city in the Western World—for the thirtieth international eucharistic congress of the Roman Catholic Church.


In the blue water of the bay, where the galleys of Rome and Carthage once battled for mastery of the seas, nearly 20 large steamships will lie at anchor from May to 11, the dates, inclusive, of the congress, after having brought 10000 pilgrims from all parts of the world.


10 Cardinals Attend.

The pilgrim ships will include the liners Rochambeau, from New York, and Araguvya, from Boston, bringing 1000 pilgrims from the United States and Canada.


A French warship has been designated to bring Cardinal Lepicier, and he will be welcomed at Tunis as an ambassador by President General Manceron of Tunisia and by the nominal ruler of the country, the Moslem Bey of Tunis.


Carthage will not receive the pilgrims with the splendor or the comfort which could be offered by many cities, says Mgr. Lamaitre Archbishop of Carthage. It will offer, on the other hand, a country which was for centuries an ensemble of ruins: of the great basilicas where St. Cyprien and St. Augustine preached; of the great gladiatorial arena where St. Perpetua, St. Felicity and thousands of others died for their faith.


5000 to Live on Ships.

The ceremonies will be divided between the Cathedral St. Louis in Carthage, the ruins surrounding Carthage and the cathedral in Tunis. Carthage now is a mere village; Tunis is a city of 186,600 inhabitants. To handle the enormous traffic between Carthage and Tunis, the electric railway connecting the two places has made special arrangements to handle 1000 passengers an hour.

FRITTERS, like waffles and pancakes, are at their best when served in the home. Nothing like a good homemade fritter, because that's the place where it can be served as it should be—direct from stove to table with not a moment lost. Fritters can't be cooked much in advance of serving, nor can they be allowed to stand. They are delicious when hot, crisp and light. But after standing for a few minutes they deteriorate. And a moist, soggy fritter isn't quite lit to eat.


The fat to be used should be heated while preparing the batter. Any vegetable fat will do, and use plenty of it—enough to float three or four fritters at a time. Heat in a deep saucepan—the rounded Scotch bowl is best—and test for temperature before putting in the fritters. Drop in a cube of bread and if it browns in so seconds the fat is hot enough. Do not increase heat or let it smoke, or the fritters will be a scorchy brown on the outside before they are cooked through.


Here is a basic recipe for fritter batter:


Plain Batter.


1 Cupful flour.


2 Teaspoonfuls baking powder.


1 Teaspoonful salt.


1 Egg.


1/2 Cup milk.


Sift together the dry ingredients. Add the beaten egg, then the milk, beating hard until smooth.


A large variety of fritters can be made using this same kind of batter. Apples in eighths, bananas, dates, slices of pineapple that are well drained, plums, prunes, and so on. Any cooked or canned fruit, however, must be well drained before using, or it will thin the batter. Drop each piece of fruit in the batter, well with a spoon, then lift into the hot fat. When light brown on one side, turn, and when browned on both sides, lift with a strainer or perforated spoon from the fat, and place on a platter spread with paper napkins to drain. Serve immediately, but keep the platter in a warm oven until ready. Do not let the fritters cool off even for a few seconds.

Sour Cream Batter.


1 Cupful flour.


1/2 Cupful sour cream.


1/4 Teaspoonful soda.


1/4 Teaspoonful salt.


2 Eggs.


Dissolve the soda in the sour cream. Mix with the beaten egg, yolk and flour and lastly fold in the stiffly beaten egg-whites.

Currant, strawberry, raspberry or any other kind of jam may be heated over water, mixed with a little lemon juice for extra tartness, and served hot. Or poured on the individual plate with a serving of fritters sent separately for each person to the table.

In order to make the new rates directly available where they are needed arrangements were made for the Department of Agriculture to certify to the railroad companies of each state where the drought is sufficiently acute to justify them. Any dealer or farmer desiring to move any of the emergency commodities reports his needs to the local county agent, who may approve or disapprove the application and notify the local station agent of the railroad. A special liaison officer in Washington handles negotiations on particular cases between the Department of Agriculture and the railroads.

It is believed that use of the county agents, who are under the Department of Agriculture, will prevent anyone taking speculative advantage of the lower rates.

Following his conference with the governors, the President met the heads of the National Grange, the Farmers union and the American Farm Bureau federation. Chairman Legge of the federal farm board also was in Washington, having hurried back from the Northwest by plane.

President Hoover announced that his plans for vacation trip to Glacier and Yellowstone national parks were cancelled and that he would remain in or near Washington to help put into effect the drought relief program, spending the week-ends at his camp on the Rapidan.

HOUSEWIVES of the country are warned not to let themselves be gouged by dealers in vegetables, fruit and other foodstuffs. There is no cause for alarm over a shortage of such commodities, and no justification for marked advance in prices except in certain localities. Congressman La Guardia called upon the President and Secretary Hyde to report that profiteers in New York city had raised prices from 20 to 15 per cent. Mr. Hyde said there would be no profiteering by the farmers, and that the government would do what it could to stop price gouging by middlemen.

Reports that barley, wheat and rye, small grain usually more costly than corn, were being substituted generally over the country for corn as feed for animals and in industrial uses, were noted. The existing barley crop of 330,000,000 bushels is almost twice the size of any barley crop produced in the last ten years. It has increased in value in recent weeks, and is being used to larger extent in dairy feeds and by farmers, chiefly in Wisconsin and Minnesota, millers reported.

Corn products manufacturers have purchased rye and barley as well as wheat in recent weeks for substitution in making industrial alcohol.

Nature did something in the way of relief, sending cooler weather and occasional rains to some parts of the corn belt.

should the lecturer become tiresome, two or
three of the locals brought in another speaker, or an
orchestra, or grand opera, or vaudeville skits,
even prize fight.

The other blow to Chautauqua was com-
pound one, delivered by one of Chautauqua's
best friends and one of Chautauqua's indomi-
table enemies. That was the lure of the motion
picture show assisted by the growing network
of good roads and the automobiles that used
them. Whereas the automobile once carried
the crowds from miles around to attend Chau-
tauqua, it later began to carry them to the
movies. The motion picture was perfected. Slapstick comedies gave way to bet-
ter-class films. Newsreels became something
to conjure with.

Then the movie and the radio combined.
The talking pictures resulted. And here, at last,
was the final blow needed to complete the down-
fall of the platform lecturer. In one film a
lecturer could record speech that would sway
50, 900, 600 persons without moving from the
studio; he could reach every hamlet with voice,
gesture and reflected personality. Month
after an important event a national hero's
opinions on it could be heard in every movie
house in America. More than that, it took
the musical comedies and the best dramas of
Broadway into the isolated districts. Small
casts presenting abbreviated versions of stand-
ard plays from Chautauqua platforms no longer
need constitute the countryman's whole dra-
matic fare.

Thus the cycle of the Chautauqua approaches
its close. Founded on the banks of a
beautiful New York lake as a means of religious
education, it became the Nation's entertain-
ment. It carried culture and learning to the
farm communities. Now it is giving way to
new developments, to science. Once it was
the last word in entertainment; now it is be-
coming a back number.

But to those who grew up on Chautauqua
there is sadness in its passing; it was an
institution of tremendous influence. Its Swiss
Bell Ringers gave an inkling of the music of
other lands. Its William Jennings Bryan
took political idealism to the common people.

BECAUSE Jack Elder was falsely
advertised as a competitor in
an Olympic sprint series the other
night and the Brooklyn college I.M.
der whose auspices he ran has been
a mountaineering organization since
1919 there has developed another
unsavory situation in amateur ath-
letics—a situation which suggests
anew that the background of most
of these scattered indoor meets is
not entirely free of commercialism.
The meet in question managed by
James Reilly, who seems to have qualified
for the assignment by reason of the fact
that he is the brother of Joseph Reilly,
former power in the administration of the
Metropolitan body of the Amateur Ath-
letic Union, otherwise the well-known.


Reilly insists the appearance of the
Notre Dame sprinter was not
falsely advertised and he shifts the
blame for the impression that the
young man would participate in the
sprint series to the newspaper men
charging that they misinterpreted
the advance publicity which he sent
to them.


None of this advance publicity
stated specifically and without
reservation that Elder would com-
pete against Karl Wildermuth, Jim
Daley and other stars in the sprint
series and when the newspaper men
accepted this information as the
facts they did so in the belief that
the source was authentic and re-
sponsible; it develops that it wasn't.


Of course it is possible that when Reilly
sent word to the newspaper offices that
Elder would race in the sprint series,
which was contrary to the truth since the
Notre Dame athlete had filed his entry
definitely in only two events, the sixty-
yard sprint and the seventy-five-yard
sprint, he did not intend that anybody
should take him seriously.


Reilly is probably an avid
reader of the sports pages and from
time to time he must have come
across certain pieces of matter al-
leged to be news that caused him
to yawn and wonder how the per-
petrators ever get away with that
sort of stuff.


When Jack Kearns was han-
dling the Dempsey fellow he
would spread the report that
group of millionaire bottle washers
in South America were bidding
against Tex Rickard for the cur-
rent battle of the century and for
some reason or other this would be
blown up into a news item of con-
siderable magnitude and the story
would receive positions of varying
importance in the sports pages, de-
pending in the main on how well
Kearns stood socially with this
sports editor or that sports editor.
I am reminded also that even the
severely decorous Gene Tunney was not
beyond subterfuge in this respect and that
on more than one occasion he authorized
the issuance of statements that were with-
out foundation in fact and were designed
wholly to expedite if not improve his ne-
gotiations with the promoter of the next
fight featuring him.


The business of sports and the
ballyhoo seem to go hand in hand
and it is not always easy for the
editor to distinguish between facts
and hooey. Quite a bit of the
ballyhoo that grows up around the
presentation of a prize fight is
harmless in nature and at times
even amusing.
In most sports departments a cer-
tain vigilance is exercised to keep
the matter within the bounds of
probability, and in recent years
the demand for novelty in training
camp guff has reached such a keen
point that the hackneyed is no
longer generally accepted.


For example, when Tommy Loughran
was claimed by his press agent to have
saved a demure miss from drowning in a
lake adjacent to his training camp last
summer, only nine of the metropolitan
dailies treated it as news, and only five
printed photographs showing the heroic
young man and the duly grateful young

vicinity of the junction of Coolidge

De Rivera's iron hand quickly stopped the domestic troubles, but it was not until two years later that the Morocco campaign succeeded and the Riff leader, Abd el Krim, was defeated, with the aid of the French.

Returning from Morocco De Rivera strove for the political regeneration of the country In December, 1925, so slowly did this program proceed, King Alfonso agreed to change the military dictatorship to a civil one.

Affairs turned somewhat to the worse, however, and the dictator learned he could no longer count on the support of a certain section of the army. Acting quickly however, in characteristic fashion, De Rivera always was able to upset counter plots. Likely he would have been overthrown had his enemies not wasted time preparing and had they been in more complete accord.

Acquittal Weakened Leader

The acquittal of Sanchez Guerra by a court-martial, despite the fact he had admitted himself guilty of framing a revolt against the government was a direct hint that De Rivera should go. Yet after lengthy cabinet meetings and several talks with King Alfonso, the dictator announced a few days ago he would continue in power another half year, or until next June. N.Y. York. Feb. 2—Two robbers, frightened when their intended victim threw milk cans through a plate glass window, fled in a automobile today and outran a pursuing taxi from which a policeman fired nine shots at them.

After a chase of more than two miles the taxi crashed into fire hydrant while trying to force the turning car into the curb. The driver injured, but the patrolman, David Wolenski, was thrown to the street and suffered fractured shoulder and a severe laceration of the scalp. The robbers escaped.
